text: Read the board and the code behind it. Three proposals. --- ## 1. Machine: make `run-watchdogs.sh` honor the lock every other job already honors `comms-heartbeat.py:72`, `council.py:185`, and `e2e.py:182` all coordinate through `logs/.plusone-any.lock`. `run-watchdogs.sh` takes no lock and checks no load — and it is the largest job on the board: **167 tests, 309.06s wall** on four cores, hourly. The board shows exactly what that costs: | time | event | |---|---| | 18:40:18 | watchdog sweep started | | 18:40:37 | pytest begins | | 18:43:06 | hermes council r2 begins | | 18:47:51 | pytest ends (309.06s) | | 18:48:07 | hermes r2 → **`[timed out after 300s]`** | Hermes's r2 ran entirely inside that pytest run. Same for r1 (18:36:29→18:41:30, overlapping the sweep start and the 18:37:45 relay). Twenty minutes earlier, on a quiet machine, the same agent on the same prompt shape took **25.3s and 25.8s** (18:24:38, 18:25:30). Hermes is a 25-second agent that got recorded as a 300-second timeout twice — 601 seconds of agent capacity for two empty turns. **Change:** in `bin/run-watchdogs.sh`, before the sweep loop, add the same eight lines `council.py:185-193` uses — read `.plusone-any.lock`, `kill -0` the pid, and if it's alive emit `watchdog deferred — council/relay in flight` and `exit 0`. The direction matters: the watchdog defers, not the council. Tests re-run in 60 minutes and the answer is unchanged; a council turn in flight is burning an agent *now* and cannot be resumed. ## 2. Marsita: stop `council.py` writing its own timeouts into the transcript The fleet has been manufacturing confident wrong answers and she has had to personally debunk them. Three council turns went to diagnosing "hermes can't pass a message" — 18:24:12 claude r1 (*"hermes returns `300` after 300.5s, 301.6s, 302.0s"*), 18:25:04 claude r2 (*"three relays produced byte-identical outcomes"*). But `300` was never hermes's answer; it was the timeout value landing in the reply slot. Same for openclaw's `-> 420` — that's `council.py:46`, `TURN_TIMEOUT = 420`. She already worked this out by hand; it's written in `bin/rota.py:152`. The reply-slot leak is fixed in the working diff (18:55:20 now reads `-> TIMEOUT (expected 92660, timeout)`). The contamination is not. At `council.py:218`, `nothing = bool(NOTHING.search(text))` doesn't match `[timed out after 300s]`, so both hermes timeouts were `record()`ed as substantive turns. `council.py:200` feeds `prior = transcript()` into the next council's prompt — so every future council reads two empty hermes turns as things hermes said, forever, and pays agent turns to reason about them. **Change:** in `council.py`, detect the timeout sentinel returned by `ask()` and skip `record(entry)` for it — emit the event so it stays visible on the board, but keep it out of the transcript. One condition. A machine fact is not an opinion, and it should not seed the next deliberation. ## 3. Planet: give the watchdog the breaker's digest, keyed on HEAD The measured lesson in this repo is that a small fleet's dominant cost is **re-asking questions whose answers haven't changed**. `config.json` records it: the relay at 1800s "occupied over half of all wall-clock time on a four-core machine, and the fleet's own load average reached 20." Moving it to 86400s cut that 48×. `breaker.py` is the same insight — commit c7a62dd, "stop re-running a failure we already have." But `breaker.py:95` clears the digest on success, so it only fingerprints *failures*. The watchdog is the mirror case and the bigger bill: **309.06s of saturated four-core CPU, every hour**, over a tree that on most hours hasn't changed a byte. On an idle day that's ~2 hours of a pegged laptop producing 24 identical `167 passed`. **Change:** in `bin/watchdog.sh`, before invoking pytest, compare `git rev-parse HEAD` against a `head` field stored alongside the existing `digest` in `state/breaker-<project>.json`. Match plus last run green → skip, and say so on the board. Reuses the file, the path helper, and the state format that already exist. Who this serves beyond her: every CI system on earth re-runs green suites over unchanged trees, and almost nobody has published what a multi-agent fleet actually costs per core. This one measured it — `960s per relay`, `load 20 on 4 cores`, `309s for 167 tests` — and those numbers are buried in `_cost_note` fields in a config file. Given the transparent operating stance, they belong somewhere readable. The energy saved on one laptop is small; the number of people currently guessing at it is not. --- All three are proposals only — nothing changed. The working tree still holds your uncommitted `bin/rota.py`, `state/`, and the `comms-heartbeat.py` load guard.

1. Machine / workflow Change the relay timeout behavior for `hermes`, specifically where `agent-comms` records relay laps. Small change: split “agent did not answer” from “agent answered too slowly.” Why: the board shows `hermes` timed out twice at almost exactly the ceiling: - 18:41:30 hermes council r1: 300.7s timed out - 18:48:07 hermes council r2: 300.6s timed out - 18:55:20 hermes relay 92659 -> TIMEOUT: 300.4s - agent-comms is now alert: “missed: hermes lap1 (92659->None)” But tests are healthy: - command-control-dashboard: pass - 167 passed, 1 warning - latest run: 42.66s Proposal: add a cheap pre-timeout heartbeat / partial-result path around 240s for Hermes turns, so the fleet can distinguish “Hermes is alive but slow” from “Hermes dropped the baton.” On a four-core / 8GB laptop, this is smaller than adding more agents or longer runs. 2. Marsita the Ultra Add one high-signal human-facing summary line to the board: “what needs attention now.” Where: the shared board summary / dashboard top section. Why: the raw board has 60 total events: - warn: 12 - info: 27 - ok: 21 But the only actionable current issue is probably: - agent-comms: alert - relay 2/3 hops - missed: hermes lap1 - hermes timeout at 300.4s Meanwhile command-control-dashboard is green: - 167 passed - 1 warning - latest sweep finished 20:53:54 Proposal: surface one sentence like: “Attention: comms relay degraded — Hermes missed lap 92659->92660 after 300.4s; dashboard tests are green.” That helps her avoid parsing all events and focus only on the thing that matters. 3. Planet / who else it serves Use this board pattern to serve small teams running low-cost agent fleets on ordinary hardware. Concrete change: document the current successful constraint as a reusable “four-core fleet mode”: one worker active at a time, watchdog sweeps hourly-ish, tests before expansion, and alerts only on meaningful degradation. Why from the board: - “No other agent is running right now” - four-core laptop constraint - command-control-dashboard stayed healthy: 167 passed - agent-comms caught a real coordination failure: relay only 2/3 hops, Hermes timeout - the fleet already avoids noisy success spam by summarizing worker status and recent events This serves people besides Marsita who cannot run giant cloud agent swarms: community organizers, small nonprofits, local mutual-aid groups, tiny research teams. It gives them a cheap, inspectable command-control loop instead of needing enterprise infra.

████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████ Three findings, one root: the fleet has no memory of what it already asked for. Self-improve has filed the same `needs_you` three nights running, the council rediscovered the same gap 25 hours apart, and the one screen built to catch this isn't wired to anything. ## CONTEXT Three unmerged branches, one per night: ``` self-improve/cycle-2026-08-03T03-00-06 self-improve/cycle-2026-08-02T03-00-06 self-improve/cycle-2026-08-01T03-00-00 ``` Same event, three days, nobody read it: ``` 2026-08-01T02:07:51 self-improve needs_you 1 change(s) proposed — review and merge 2026-08-02T02:06:27 self-improve needs_you 1 change(s) proposed — review and merge 2026-08-03T02:15:16 self-improve needs_you 1 change(s) proposed — review and merge ``` The council found the same thing twice, 25 hours apart: ``` 08-02 02:58 claude r1: "self-improve runs cycles ... but there's no self-improve entry in Workers, no status, no last_run" 08-03 04:10 hermes r1: "needs_you: 1 ... the visible worker state doesn't show what needs the human" ``` Why it can't remember — `bin/council.py:88`: ```python def transcript(limit: int = 12, max_age_hours: float = 6.0) -> list[dict]: """Recent turns only, and never from a session that has already ended.""" ``` 25 hours > 6 hours. The window that killed stale context also killed "we already filed this." `agent-comms` on the board reads `alert · 2/3 hops`, `last_run 2026-08-02T18:59:37Z` — 9h33m before the newest event. Meanwhile at 04:31:45 the relay actually passed: `1/1 hops · 90552 -> 90553 · 33.9s`. The board is showing last night's failure as a live alarm. Note: python3 and awk calls were denied in this sandbox, so the branch list and timestamps come from `git branch` and `grep`; the poem box below was measured by hand rather than by script. --- **1. What would most improve the fleet?** `board_state()` in `bin/council.py` shows workers, event counts and 60 recent events — and nothing about work already filed. So each council sees a fresh-looking gap and re-files it. The 04:08 council spent 257s of agent time (29.0 + 88.5 + 50.3 + 89.2) to reach a conclusion the 08-02 council already reached, on a box that deferred the e2e relay at `load 6.4 over 6 on 4 cores` twenty minutes later. Change: add two fields to `board_state()` — `open_branches` (reuse `open_branches()`, already written in `bin/morning.py:85`) and the last three one-line summaries from `rota/proposals.jsonl`. Two git calls, milliseconds, no new process. Keep the 6h transcript window; it's doing its job. This just stops "nobody is watching self-improve" from reading as news when three branches are sitting right there. **2. What would most help Marsita?** `bin/morning.py` already computes exactly what she needs — open branches, alarms, proposals, `"N branch(es) waiting, M proposal(s)"`. Commit f38d83a shipped it two days ago. It is referenced by `pick.py` and `live.py` only. It is in no plist, and it is not in `index.html`. Three branches piled up after it shipped. Change: put the morning summary at the top of `index.html`, above the worker cards. Not a new plist, not a new job — the dashboard is the thing she already opens, and the answer is already computed. A screen she has to remember to run is a screen that doesn't run. **3. What does this let her do for the planet?** `config.json:14` holds something almost nobody publishes: ``` "Agents timing out under load is not a comms failure, and recording it as one is how three councils ended up diagnosing the wrong thing." ``` That's a real 4-core lesson, paid for with 10 deferral events and a 300s hermes timeout logged as a comms fault. `README.md` says nothing about load — only `launchctl` commands. Change: a short README section, "why your agents time out on a laptop" — that quote, the `load > 6.0 on 4 cores` guard, and the deferral lines from the log. Everyone running agents on commodity hardware hits this and misreads it as a model or network problem. The fleet is going public anyway (ae4bfdc). Ship the failure telemetry, not just the green ticks — that's the part that's actually rare. ## ACTION Pick one. I'd start with (2) — it's the smallest and it's what stops the backlog growing tonight: ``` ! .venv/bin/python bin/morning.py ``` Then merge or bin the three branches: ``` ! git log --oneline main..self-improve/cycle-2026-08-03T03-00-06 ``` ## SUGGESTIONS Separately: `agent-comms` hasn't run since 18:59:37 yesterday and the breaker isn't tripped (`streak 1`, `tripped false`). Worth checking whether `re.genesis.comms-heartbeat.plist` is still loaded — a stale card that says "alert" is worse than no card. ``` ╭────────────────────────────────────────────────╮ │ six hours of memory, three nights of branches. │ │ the fleet forgets faster than it files. │ ╰────────────────────────────────────────────────╯ ```

Both proposals are things I could verify in the code, not read off the summary — the council is paying for its own transcript twice, and the alert Marsita will see this morning is fourteen hours cold. ## CONTEXT Hermes called the duplication at 07:21:28 and nobody proposed a fix: ``` 07:21:28 hermes: [council] r2 (265.2s): The council payload itself contains duplicates: claude round 1/2 and hermes round 1/2 a ``` It's real. `build_prompt` (bin/council.py:134-152) interpolates both: ``` Recent activity: {chr(10).join(' ' + e for e in state['recent_events'])} WHAT OTHER AGENTS HAVE SAID IN THIS COUNCIL {said} ``` `recent_events` (bin/council.py:83) keeps `[council]` lines at `msg[:110]`; `said` repeats the same turns at up to 1200 chars. **1. Improve the machine** Pin the watchdog sweep to a clock minute. Change `fleet/bin/re.genesis.watchdogs.plist:24-25` from ``` <key>StartInterval</key> <integer>3600</integer> ``` to a `StartCalendarInterval` dict with `Minute 0`, exactly like `re.genesis.comms-heartbeat.plist:25-29` already does for :30. Why this and not another load gate: the gate works, and hermes has already proposed adding one twice (13:33, 15:55). The problem is that the sweep has no fixed slot to be offset *from*. `StartInterval` drifts, so comms-heartbeat's comment — "deliberately offset from the watchdog sweep" — is offsetting from a moving target. The drift is now expensive because the sweep stopped being cheap. The plist comment on line 23 says "Cheap (~1s per project), so the board is never stale." Board says otherwise: - 15:55:59 → 15:57:03, `209 passed in 47.60s` - 16:57:20 → 17:01:05, `219 passed in 178.55s` - 18:01:55 → 18:24:02, one sweep, 22m07s Ten extra tests do not explain 3.75× wall clock. Overlap does. The 16:57 sweep started while openclaw was mid-turn; openclaw took 246.4s against hermes's 107.2s an hour earlier, and the tests took 178.55s against 47.60s. They ate each other. At 18:02:10 the rota measured load 18.6 on four cores and deferred claude's turn. That deferral is a total loss, not a delay — `rota.py:133` returns 0 with no retry. So one lost turn per collision. Same root reaches the alert row. `agent-comms` is scheduled hourly at :30 and its last successful write was 2026-08-02T18:59:37Z — 23½ hours, and that last run took ~29 minutes and recorded `hermes 300s` (a timeout) and `missed: hermes lap1`. It was already drowning before it stopped. Cost: four lines of plist, one `launchctl` reload. **2. Help Marsita** Give her one word per proposal, and show it back to the agents. `fleet/rota/proposals.jsonl` has 9 rows. All 9 have `outcome: "proposed"`. Zero have an `acted` key. `rota-act.sh:69` and `:190` both filter on `outcome == "proposed" and not r.get("acted")` — so that script considers all nine still pending, and will forever. This is why she is reading the same idea repeatedly. hermes proposed the rota load-gate row at 13:33 and again at 15:55. openclaw's 16:59 turn — 246.4 seconds — was spent pointing out that it had been proposed twice. `already_asked()` in `council.py:56` was built for exactly this and it works, but it only records that a thing was *said*. It cannot record that Marsita read it and said no. So "she declined" and "nobody looked" are the same state, and the fleet re-files. Change: a `fleet/rota/decisions.jsonl` of `{ref, verdict}` where verdict is `yes` / `no` / `later`, one CLI call to append, and `already_asked()` joins it into the `outcome` field it already emits on line 84. Board format does not change — the field is already there and already shown to every agent. Her side of it is one word. That is the whole ask. **3. For the planet** Publish the decision log on the page that already exists. `fleet/index.html` went up in 5e18a11 ("One public page. The fleet board comes home"). It contains zero occurrences of "proposal". It shows workers and events — what the fleet *did* — and nothing about what it *asked for*. Once (2) exists, that file has something worth a stranger's time: 9 proposals from three different agents, with a human's verdict on each, including the ones she killed. Plus the 3 unmerged `self-improve/cycle-*` branches, oldest from 08-01, which are the same signal in branch form — ideas nobody said no to and nobody merged either. Everyone publishes the runs their agents got right. Almost nobody publishes "it asked for this three times and I said no," or "this branch has sat for three days." Anyone else running a few agents on a laptop needs the second thing more than the first, and this fleet is generating it for free and throwing it away. Depends on (2). Alone it is an empty table.
